newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU uncertainty prompts debate over strategies.
newsitem.headline: EMU uncertainty prompts debate over strategies.

text.p: The fate of the European Union's budget stability pact for countries inside monetary union and Germany's ruling coalition are perhaps the two biggest uncertainties facing the planned single currency, analysts said on Tuesday.

Although many still reckon the odds favour a timely launch of the euro on January 1, 1999, the way EU leaders and policy-makers manoeuvre around these potential landmines could determine whether investor confidence in the euro remains intact.
"The next month is probably the most critical one in the whole process," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Manhattan Bank in London.

Already, a modest shift in sentiment appears to have developed in favour of delaying the ambitious project. The German mark rose against the dollar and most European currencies on Monday after France asked its EU partners for more time to study the stability pact.
Peripheral markets, such as Spain and Portugal, were also hit, surprising some analysts who believed a soft euro -- one with a large number of initial members -- was the mostly likely scenario.

"The knee-jerk reaction yesterday was to buy marks," said one trading manager at a large German bank in London. He saidItaly would perhaps suffer most should the EU decide on a new starting date for EMU.
Others disagreed, stressing that Italy's long process of economic and budgetary reform would likely continue in the face of EMU's worst crisis.

"Even in a chaos nightmare event we still like the spread of Italy or Spain, because if you pretend monetary union never existed you're back to fundamentals," Mark Fox, chief European strategist at Lehman Brothers, told Reuters Financial Television.
The split among analysts and traders over whether there would be value in southern European economies following a delay to EMU centred on a judgment of political will.
Those who believe the Italian lira would plummet under such circumstances forecast political instability would ensue almost immediately.
"If there is a real delay the Italians are going to be the first to go because they don't have the political will and support to carry on for another few years," added the German trading manager.

Regarding EMU's stability pact, analysts said markets were for the moment giving policy-makers the benefit of the doubt. Many expect to see a deal brokered with France that would allow the accord to be wrapped up shortly after the EU summit in Amsterdam next week.

Among options discussed by EU finance ministers on Monday in Luxembourg, one stood out -- a protocol or resolution attached to the stability pact that would emphasise the key French demand of jobs growth.

However, if French officials, under pressure from the National Assembly, believe they have to renegotiate some of the pact's more important elements, such as fines for countries exceeding deficit limits, then all bets are off.
"If the stability pact gets reopened, then I think the markets will get more nervous," said Marshall of Chase Manhattan Bank.
France's National Assembly is due to review the EU budget accord on June 19.
Another major worry is the German political situation.

Irrespective of what happens in France, many analysts said the euro's ultimate fate rests with Chancellor Helmut Kohl and whether his ruling coalition can withstand both an internal battle and a bruising encounter with the opposition.

Should Kohl and his coalition collapse, which is still seen as unlikely, then a rapid flight to quality would develop, benefiting the dollar or perhaps other safe-haven currencies such as the Swiss franc.

The safe-haven play, however, is also controversial among strategists, with some reckoning that the less than stellar fundamentals of the Swiss economy would eventually wipe out any gains the franc might see from EMU turmoil.
